  • Can you have a vaginal birth after a cesarean?
Pregnancy

Can you have a vaginal birth after a cesarean?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A previous cesarean does not always mean you need another one. Discussing your options early gives the maternity team time to review the operation record, assess the current pregnancy and build a plan that reflects your preferences.

A previous cesarean does not settle the next birth plan

Vaginal birth after cesarean, or VBAC, means giving birth vaginally after an earlier cesarean. A trial of labour after cesarean, often shortened to TOLAC, is the plan to labour with that possibility in mind. If vaginal birth occurs, it is a VBAC; if concerns arise, an unplanned cesarean may be needed. These terms distinguish the plan from the eventual outcome.

Many people can consider either planned labour or a planned repeat cesarean, while others have medical reasons that make one option preferable. The discussion should include your previous birth, current pregnancy, preferences and available care. An uncomplicated vaginal birth can avoid another abdominal operation and shorten recovery. Choosing surgery, or needing it during labour, is not a failure.

Understand the likelihood in the right context

RCOG estimates that about three in four people with one previous cesarean whose labour starts spontaneously have a vaginal birth. A previous vaginal birth, whether before or after the cesarean, improves the likelihood; the estimate is around eight to nine in ten in that group. These are group figures and cannot guarantee how your labour will unfold.

A previous vaginal birth is therefore helpful information, but it is not a prerequisite. The reason for the earlier operation, the current baby’s position and other pregnancy factors also matter. Ask which features of your own history change the discussion. A prediction tool, if used, should support a conversation about options rather than become the sole basis for denying one.

Review the operation record and the uterine scar

The cut in the uterus matters more than the appearance of the skin scar. A low transverse uterine incision runs across the lower uterus and is common in modern cesarean birth. It often permits consideration of labour in a later pregnancy. The outside scar cannot reliably tell you whether that was the incision used; ask the team to obtain the operation report if possible.

A classical incision in the upper uterus, a previous uterine rupture or some other operations that cut through the uterine wall can substantially change the recommendation. An uncertain scar history needs specialist review rather than a guess from a photograph. After more than one cesarean, an individual discussion is also needed; the number, type of scars and local expertise all contribute.

Consider the current pregnancy as well as the previous one

A straightforward singleton pregnancy with the baby head down is a common setting for planned VBAC. Estimated size, placental position, gestational age and the reason for the first cesarean can affect the balance. A previous label such as “baby too large” or “labour did not progress” needs review in context rather than being treated as proof that every future baby must be born by surgery.

Diabetes, high blood pressure or a history of genital herpes are not interchangeable, automatic exclusions. The severity, current findings and effect on timing or route of birth matter. For example, active genital infection around labour requires a different discussion from a past history alone. Twins or a suspected large baby also require specialist assessment rather than a universal yes-or-no checklist. A placenta covering the cervix is a separate reason vaginal birth may be unsafe.

Compare labour risks with the risks of another operation

One concern with labour after cesarean is that the uterine scar may open, called uterine rupture. RCOG describes a risk of up to about one in two hundred in its patient information; the figure varies with circumstances. Rupture is uncommon but can cause severe bleeding and serious harm to the baby, requiring urgent surgery. Labour may also end in an unplanned cesarean for other reasons.

A planned repeat cesarean reduces the risk of rupture during labour but brings surgical risks, including infection, bleeding, clots, injury to nearby organs and a longer recovery. Repeated operations can create adhesions and raise the risk of abnormal placental attachment in later pregnancies. A vaginal birth can involve an assisted birth or a perineal tear. Compare the whole balance with your team, including your plans for more children.

Induction is a specialist discussion, not an automatic prohibition

Some people can have induction after a previous cesarean, but the method and reason matter. It can reduce the chance of vaginal birth and increase the risk of scar rupture; RCOG describes a roughly two- to three-fold increase depending on how labour is started. Some medicines used to prepare the cervix are unsuitable after a uterine scar. Ask which options are available in your circumstances.

If labour has not started by the agreed review date, or birth is recommended earlier for a medical reason, discuss waiting, induction and planned cesarean together. Do not attempt home methods to induce labour. The plan should state when to contact the maternity unit if contractions start or the waters break, and how the team will reassess if the situation changes.

Choose care with monitoring and emergency capacity

Planned labour after cesarean should take place in a setting equipped to respond promptly if surgery is needed. NICE recommends electronic fetal monitoring, immediate access to cesarean birth and on-site blood transfusion services. Changes in the baby’s heart-rate pattern can be an early sign of a scar problem. Ask what monitoring means for movement, positioning and the birth support you want.

Discuss pain relief, including an epidural if desired, and the circumstances in which the team would recommend changing the plan. If a local unit does not offer VBAC, ask whether this reflects your individual medical situation or the unit’s resources. An early referral or second opinion may clarify options. Emergency capacity is part of the plan, even when a previous birth story makes vaginal birth seem straightforward.

Put historical access figures in context

A United States NIH consensus conference in 2010 examined why access to labour after cesarean had become restricted. Reports from that period described VBAC rates falling from more than twenty-eight percent in 1996 to around eight percent by the time of the review. Those are historical figures about use of VBAC, not today’s rates or the chance of vaginal birth for an individual who attempts labour.

The conference discussion included hospital policies, professional concerns, liability and resources as well as clinical safety. This helps explain why availability may differ between services. It does not establish that a fixed percentage of current clinicians refuse VBAC or that a hospital’s recommendation is necessarily wrong. Ask for an explanation of the present local policy and how it applies to you.

Put personal birth stories in context

One reported birth story describes a parent whose first cesarean followed concern that the pelvis was too small. After becoming pregnant again about a year later, she asked to try labour despite an initial recommendation for another operation. The account describes a vaginal birth at forty weeks without reported complications. It illustrates why someone may wish to revisit the earlier explanation, but it is an anecdote rather than a verified medical record.

Another person’s outcome cannot show whether your scar, pregnancy spacing or current baby makes labour appropriate. Use stories to develop questions, not to decide that persistence guarantees safety. Midwives, nurses, antenatal educators and supportive relatives can help you prepare for the discussion. If the first birth was distressing, ask for a birth review or emotional support as well as a clinical plan.

Make the decision early and leave room to revisit it

Bring your questions to early antenatal visits: what was the reason for the previous operation, what type of uterine incision was used, what are the benefits and risks now, and where can the chosen plan be supported? If this is your first pregnancy, understanding why a cesarean is proposed and how it might affect future pregnancies can still be useful. Avoid treating all first cesareans as unnecessary; some are lifesaving and preferences deserve respectful discussion.

For a planned repeat cesarean, the team commonly schedules birth at or after thirty-nine weeks unless there is a reason for earlier delivery. Ask what happens if labour begins before that date. For planned VBAC, agree how long to wait for spontaneous labour and when the plan will be reviewed. Your decision can change as information or preferences change, and the final aim remains care that is informed, responsive and respectful.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

RCOG and ACOG support individual discussion of vaginal birth and repeat cesarean after a previous operation.

NICE recommends appropriate monitoring and immediate access to emergency surgery and transfusion for planned labour after cesarean.

How BeMama can help

Bring the earlier operation details and a short list of questions to an antenatal appointment. Ask for a written plan for labour, induction decisions and unexpected changes.

When to seek help

Follow the maternity unit’s advice about contacting them when contractions begin or waters break. Seek urgent assessment for severe persistent pain, bleeding, reduced fetal movement or feeling acutely unwell.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Previous vaginal birth improves the likelihood but is not required.
  • The uterine incision cannot be identified from the skin scar.
  • Current pregnancy conditions need individual assessment.
  • Induction may be possible with specialist planning.
  • Compare both birth options and ensure emergency care is available.

Frequently asked questions

Must I already have had a vaginal birth to try VBAC?

No. A previous vaginal birth improves the likelihood, but it is not a requirement. The team considers your uterine scar, previous operation, current pregnancy and available care.

Does the three-in-four estimate guarantee my outcome?

No. It describes a group with one previous cesarean and spontaneous labour. Your own circumstances may differ, and a plan for labour includes the possibility of an unplanned cesarean.

Can I identify my uterine incision from my skin scar?

No. The skin incision and uterine incision may differ. Ask the team to review the previous operation report instead of judging from the outside scar.

Can VBAC be considered after two cesareans?

It may be considered in selected situations after specialist discussion. The type and number of scars, other pregnancy factors and the maternity service’s resources matter. A simple online checklist cannot establish suitability.

Is induction always forbidden after a cesarean?

No. It can be an option, but it changes the risk discussion and some induction medicines are unsuitable. The reason, method, monitoring and emergency arrangements need specialist planning.

Do diabetes or high blood pressure automatically rule it out?

Not automatically. The condition’s severity, complications and effect on the timing or route of birth need individual assessment. A past diagnosis alone does not provide the complete answer.

Why is continuous monitoring usually recommended?

Changes in the baby’s heart-rate pattern can warn of problems, including a uterine scar complication. Ask how the monitoring will work and what options you have for movement and pain relief.

What if my hospital does not offer VBAC?

Ask whether the reason is your medical situation or the service’s resources. Early discussion may allow referral or a second opinion where appropriate, while keeping emergency-care requirements in the plan.

Does another parent’s successful VBAC show mine will be safe?

No. A story may help you prepare questions, but it cannot establish your scar type, pregnancy risks or likely outcome. The birth plan should be based on your own assessment and preferences.

What if labour starts before my planned repeat cesarean?

Contact your maternity unit promptly and follow the agreed plan. The team will assess labour, your condition and the baby, then discuss the safest available options with you.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
